edges.title: Zelter’s teaching of Fanny Mendelssohn: counterpoint and Bach

works.from: Carl Friedrich Zelter, composition lessons from 1819; letter to Goethe, 1816
works.to: Fanny Mendelssohn playing the 24 preludes of the Well-Tempered Clavier from memory (1819)

edges.claim: [[fanny-hensel]] and her brother [[mendelssohn]] began composition lessons in 1819 with Carl Friedrich Zelter, head of the Berlin Sing-Akademie; Ludwig Berger had earlier taught them piano. In 1816 Zelter had written to Goethe that her father’s eldest daughter “could give you something of Sebastian Bach”. At fourteen she played all twenty-four preludes of the Well-Tempered Clavier from memory for her father’s birthday in 1819.

edges.title: Chopin and the village musicians at Szafarnia, 1825

works.from: Folk songs and dances of the Dobrzyń land, heard at Szafarnia, summers 1824 and 1825
works.to: Chopin’s mazurkas, from Op. 6 and Op. 7 (composed 1830–31, published 1832)

edges.claim: [[chopin]] spent the summers of 1824 and 1825 at Szafarnia, the Dziewanowski estate, writing down songs and joining the village musicians. In a letter home of 26 August 1825, he described accompanying a fiddler on a one-stringed cello. His first published mazurkas, Op. 6 and Op. 7, were written in 1830–31 and appeared in 1832.
edges.note: Chopin’s letters document the Szafarnia summers. Liszt’s 1852 account linked the mazurkas with Polish national music; later writers understood this as village folk music, while recent scholarship emphasises urban traditions. Which tunes, if any, Chopin took from Szafarnia remains unresolved.

works.to: Mendelssohn, Overture, Op. 21 (finished 6 August 1826); incidental music, Op. 61 (1842–43)

edges.claim: After reading August Wilhelm Schlegel’s German translation of A Midsummer Night’s Dream, made with Ludwig Tieck’s help, [[mendelssohn]] finished the concert overture, Op. 21, on 6 August 1826, at the age of seventeen years and six months. It was first played at Stettin on 20 February 1827. In 1843 he wrote incidental music for a production at Potsdam, first performed on 14 October, and incorporated the overture into it. The incidental music includes the Wedding March.

works.to: Chopin, Variations on “Là ci darem la mano”, Op. 2, piano and orchestra (1827)

edges.claim: At seventeen [[chopin]] wrote a set of variations for piano and orchestra on the duet sung by Don Giovanni and Zerlina in [[mozart]]’s opera, and dedicated it to his schoolfriend Tytus Woyciechowski; it was published in 1830. [[schumann]], who practised it for months, wrote of it through his alter ego Eusebius in the Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung of 7 December 1831, with the words “Hats off, gentlemen”. Chopin thought less of the Leipzig reviews than Schumann did of the variations. Of Friedrich Wieck’s notice in Caecilia he wrote that Wieck, “instead of being clever, is very stupid”.

edges.title: Berlioz sees Hamlet at the Odéon, 1827

works.from: Hamlet and Romeo and Juliet, Odéon, Paris, 11 and 15 September 1827
works.to: Roméo et Juliette, Op. 17 (1839); Béatrice et Bénédict (1862)

edges.claim: On 11 September 1827 [[berlioz]] saw Hamlet at the Odéon with Harriet Smithson as Ophelia; on 15 September he saw her as Juliet. In the Mémoires (chapter 18) he called the evening the “greatest drama” of his life and wrote that Shakespeare, arriving unawares, struck him like a thunderbolt. He married Smithson in 1833. The largest of his works drawn from the plays are Roméo et Juliette (1839) and Béatrice et Bénédict (1862, after Much Ado About Nothing).

edges.title: Berlioz and Habeneck’s Beethoven at the Conservatoire

works.from: Beethoven’s symphonies, Société des concerts du Conservatoire (first concert 9 March 1828)
works.to: Symphonie fantastique, Op. 14 (premiere 5 December 1830)

edges.claim: The Société des concerts du Conservatoire, directed by François Habeneck, gave its first concert on 9 March 1828, and from then on Paris heard [[beethoven]]’s symphonies played regularly. In his Mémoires (chapter 20) [[berlioz]] wrote that the shock was nearly equal to Shakespeare’s, and that Beethoven had opened a new world in music as the poet had opened one in poetry. From 1828 he also studied and copied Beethoven’s scores in the Conservatoire library. Two years later Habeneck conducted the premiere of the Symphonie fantastique in the same hall.

edges.title: Mendelssohn’s St Matthew Passion performance, Berlin, 1829

works.from: Bach, St Matthew Passion, BWV 244
works.to: Mendelssohn’s revival, Berlin Sing-Akademie, 11 March 1829

edges.claim: [[mendelssohn]]’s grandmother Bella Salomon had given him a copy of the St Matthew Passion score in the mid-1820s, and his teacher Carl Friedrich Zelter, head of the Sing-Akademie, held a store of Bach scores but would not perform the work in public. On 11 March 1829, aged twenty, Mendelssohn conducted the Passion at the Sing-Akademie in Berlin, the first performance outside Leipzig. He cut about a third of the arias and half the choruses but few chorales. The performance is usually counted as the start of the Bach revival.

works.from: Goethe, Faust Part One, in Gérard de Nerval’s French translation (1828)

edges.claim: [[berlioz]] first read Goethe’s Faust in Gérard de Nerval’s prose translation and wrote in the Mémoires (chapter 26) that he could not put it down, reading it at table, in the theatre and in the street. He set the translation’s verse fragments as Huit scènes de Faust, had them engraved at his own expense in 1829, then collected and destroyed the copies; the “Concert des Sylphes” was sung at his Conservatoire concert of 1 November 1829. Twenty years later he reworked this material into La damnation de Faust, first given at the Opéra-Comique on 6 December 1846.

edges.title: Schumann’s Papillons and the masked ball in Flegeljahre

works.from: Jean Paul, Flegeljahre (1804–05), final masked-ball chapters
works.to: Schumann, Papillons, Op. 2 (1829–31)

edges.claim: In April 1832 [[schumann]] explained to the editor Ludwig Rellstab how his Papillons arose. He asked Rellstab to recall the last scene of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre, with the masked ball, the dancing, the exchange of masks, the confessions and the brother’s departure. He said he kept turning to the last page, “almost unconsciously” found himself at the piano, and one piece after another came into being. In November 1829 he had written to Friedrich Wieck that Schubert was “my only Schubert” just as Jean Paul was “my only Jean Paul”.

edges.claim: [[liszt]], not yet twenty-one, heard Paganini on 22 April 1832 at an Opéra benefit for victims of the cholera epidemic. On 2 May he wrote to Pierre Wolff that he was practising exercises “four or five hours” a day and studying a long shelf of authors and composers at once. The first result was the Grande fantaisie de bravoure sur La Clochette (1832); the six Paganini études were published in 1838 and revised in 1851, with five based on Paganini’s Caprices.
edges.note: Some sources date the concert 20 April; this account follows 22 April.

edges.claim: [[chopin]] dedicated his twelve Op. 10 études, published in 1833, “to my friend Franz Liszt”; the second set, Op. 25, went to Liszt’s companion Marie d’Agoult. That June, in a letter to Ferdinand Hiller, Chopin wrote that he did not know what his pen was scribbling because Liszt was playing his études at that moment, and that he wished he could steal from Liszt the way to play them.

works.from: Byron, Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage (1812–18)
works.to: Harold en Italie, Op. 16, for viola and orchestra (premiere 23 November 1834)

edges.claim: Paganini asked [[berlioz]] for a showpiece for his Stradivari viola, then rejected the first movement because the viola rested too long. Berlioz kept the plan but made the solo a “melancholy dreamer in the manner of Byron’s Childe Harold”, set among his memories of the Abruzzi, and named the symphony Harold en Italie. As in the Fantastique, a theme recurs; the viola theme is laid over the orchestra’s tunes and does not interrupt them. The first performance was at the Conservatoire on 23 November 1834.

works.from: Chopin, Nocturne in D♭, Op. 27 No. 2, played at Friedrich Wieck’s house, Leipzig, September 1835
works.to: Mendelssohn’s letter to his sister Fanny

edges.claim: In September 1835 [[chopin]] visited Leipzig, where he played at Friedrich Wieck’s house and met both [[schumann]] and [[mendelssohn]]. He played the D♭ Nocturne, which was then new; Mendelssohn wrote to his sister [[fanny-hensel]] that Chopin “has also such a lovely new notturno, a considerable part of which I learnt by ear”. The two Op. 27 nocturnes were published the following year in Leipzig, Paris and London.

edges.claim: Clara Wieck began her Piano Concerto at thirteen, in January 1833. Robert Schumann revised the orchestration of its first movement in 1834; she later undid his changes, orchestrated it herself, and finished the three-movement concerto on 1 September 1835, twelve days before her sixteenth birthday. edges.title: Schumann’s Fantasie and a Beethoven song quotation

works.to: Schumann, Fantasie in C, Op. 17, first movement, closing bars (1836; published 1839)

edges.claim: [[schumann]] began the Fantasie in 1836 as Ruines, written in his distress at being parted from Clara Wieck. He expanded it to raise money for the Beethoven monument in Bonn, offering the publisher Kistner 100 presentation copies. At the end of the first movement he quoted Beethoven’s song Nimm sie hin denn, diese Lieder – ‘Accept, then, these songs’. The published score of 1839 is dedicated to [[liszt]].

edges.claim: [[liszt]] began transcribing the Fifth Symphony around the end of 1835, and by mid-1837 he had finished Nos. 5, 6 and 7 for solo piano. The Fifth and Sixth were published in 1840 with a dedication to the painter Ingres. Twenty-three years later Breitkopf & Härtel asked him to continue, and all nine appeared together in 1865, dedicated to Hans von Bülow. He had made a two-piano version of the Ninth in 1850, and at first he doubted that its finale could be arranged effectively for one piano.

works.to: Schumann, Davidsbündlertänze, Op. 6, No. 1, “Motto by C. W.” (1837)

edges.claim: Clara Wieck and [[schumann]] became secretly engaged on 14 August 1837, against her father’s opposition; within a week he began the Davidsbündlertänze. The opening bars, headed “Motto by C. W.”, quote the start of the mazurka that is No. 5 of her Soirées musicales, Op. 6, and he began to sketch a whole piece on her theme. edges.claim: Paganini, by then voiceless, heard Harold en Italie for the first time at [[berlioz]]’s Conservatoire concert of 16 December 1838, and had his son Achille relay his admiration. Two days later he wrote that with Beethoven dead only Berlioz could revive him, and sent 20,000 francs through the Baron de Rothschild. The money cleared Berlioz’s debts and left him free to compose. Roméo et Juliette was given three times, on 24 November, 1 and 15 December 1839.

edges.claim: [[chopin]] spent the winter of 1838–39 at Valldemossa, Majorca, where he had a copy of the Well-Tempered Clavier and finished his Op. 28 preludes, a cycle through all twenty-four keys. He ordered them differently from Bach, by the circle of fifths with each major key followed by its relative minor, and wrote no fugues. In January 1839 [[schumann]] visited Schubert’s brother Ferdinand in Vienna and found a copy of the manuscript among the composer’s papers; he took a copy back to Leipzig and sent it to [[mendelssohn]], who conducted the first complete public performance with the Gewandhaus Orchestra on 21 March 1839. Schumann’s article in the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik praised the symphony’s “heavenly length”, likening it to a four-volume novel, perhaps by Jean Paul.

Through Mendelssohn, Berlioz was invited to Leipzig in 1843, where he gave Gewandhaus concerts on 4 and 22 February. The two exchanged batons “as a token of friendship”, but Berlioz noted that Mendelssohn praised his romances and said nothing of the symphonies, overtures or Requiem.

edges.claim: Both [[schumann]] and [[liszt]] wrote works on the four-note motif that spells Bach’s name in German notation, and both helped found the Bach-Gesellschaft in 1850. Schumann finished his Six Fugues on the name BACH in November 1845. He called them the work that he believed would outlive his others, and said he had tried to make them worthy of the great name they bear. The first fugue introduces the four notes slowly and builds from a sombre exposition. The second compresses the subject and adds Baroque semiquaver figures.

In 1872 Wagner conducted it at Bayreuth’s Margravial Opera House for the laying of the Festspielhaus foundation stone.

edges.title: Berlioz’s Witches’ Sabbath and Liszt’s Totentanz

works.from: Berlioz, Symphonie fantastique, V: Dies irae from bar 127, bassoons and ophicleides (1830)
works.to: Liszt, Totentanz: Paraphrase on Dies irae, S. 126, piano and orchestra (completed 1849)

edges.claim: In the finale of the Symphonie fantastique, Berlioz gave the Dies irae chant to four bassoons and two ophicleides in C minor from bar 127, as a parody of the funeral rite at the witches’ sabbath. [[liszt]] met Berlioz on the day before the premiere on 5 December 1830, and in 1833 he made the piano transcription of the symphony. His Totentanz, a set of variations for piano and orchestra on the same chant, was planned in 1838, completed in 1849 and revised in 1853 and 1859. A second recorded source is the Triumph of Death fresco in the Campo Santo at Pisa, which Liszt saw in 1838.
edges.note: Both works are documented; no letter or statement has been found in which Liszt names the Fantastique as the source of the Dies irae idea. He knew the symphony intimately. The other recorded stimulus for the Totentanz is the Pisa fresco.

In the same letter he announced Tristan und Isolde: never having known the true bliss of love, he would “erect a monument to the most beautiful of all my dreams”, a conception he called the simplest but most full-blooded imaginable, ending under a black flag. edges.claim: In 1860 [[brahms]] and Joseph Joachim signed a manifesto against the “pursuits of a certain party” whose organ was Brendel’s Neue Zeitschrift für Musik. The text leaked, the journal parodied it on 4 May, and the Echo published it two days later with more than twenty names. In Vienna Brahms nevertheless helped prepare [[wagner]]’s concerts of 1862–63 and played him the Handel Variations in January 1863. Wagner gave him part of the Tannhäuser manuscript, then demanded it back in 1875.
edges.note: Brahms probably wrote the manifesto; he certainly signed it.

edges.title: Berlioz on the Tristan prelude: “reads and re-reads”

works.from: Wagner, Tristan und Isolde, Act I prelude (concert at the Salle Ventadour, February 1860)

edges.claim: Wagner’s Paris concerts of January–February 1860 included the Tristan prelude, and [[berlioz]] reviewed them in the Journal des Débats on 9 February. He described a slow piece that starts pianissimo, swells to fortissimo and falls back, with “no theme other than a sort of chromatic moaning” over dissonances whose long appoggiaturas replace the real note of the harmony. He said he had read the “strange page” again and again, listened with full attention, and still could not tell what the composer meant. Wagner, who had sent him the Tristan score early in 1860, answered with an open letter in the same paper on 22 February.

edges.claim: [[mussorgsky]]’s idea of setting Gogol’s comedy Marriage came from the advice and example of Alexander Dargomyzhsky, who in 1866 began The Stone Guest, declaring that Pushkin’s text would be set “just as it stands, so that the inner truth of the text should not be distorted”. edges.title: Wagner’s visit to Rossini in Paris

works.from: Rossini’s conversation with Wagner, Paris, March 1860
works.to: Wagner’s preface to the French prose translation of his opera poems

edges.claim: After conducting extracts from his operas in Paris early in 1860, [[wagner]] found a bon mot going round the papers: when Rossini’s friend Mercadante spoke up for Wagner’s music, Rossini had supposedly served him only the sauce of a fish. Rossini denied the story in a public letter, and Wagner called on him. He was received as a friend and heard Rossini say, in a long conversation, that he might have achieved something had he been born and educated in Germany, but that Italy in his youth had left no room for serious aims in opera. Wagner left with the impression of the first truly great man worthy of reverence he had met in the art world, and never saw him again. He wrote that in the preface to the French prose translation of his opera poems, his estimate of modern Italian opera was guided largely by what Rossini had told him from his own experience.

edges.title: Rossini’s account of Beethoven’s advice, Vienna

works.from: Beethoven’s words to Rossini as Rossini reported them, Vienna, April 1822
works.to: Rossini’s Vienna performances, beginning with Zelmira at the Kärntnertortheater, 13 April 1822

edges.claim: [[rossini]] went to Vienna in the spring of 1822 for performances of his operas that began with Zelmira at the Kärntnertortheater on 13 April. In 1860 he told Wagner what happened when he called on [[beethoven]]. Beethoven greeted him as the author of Il barbiere di Siviglia, congratulated him on an excellent opera buffa and told him never to try anything but comic opera, since serious opera was not in the nature of Italians. Edmond Michotte wrote the conversation down and published it in 1906. The story is one of the tales Rossini circulated in old age. The Fondazione Rossini has since examined the sources and concludes that the visit never took place, and that in Vienna Rossini met only Beethoven’s brother and told him how much he wished to meet Ludwig.
edges.note: The only source for the visit is Rossini’s own recollection of 1860, written up by Edmond Michotte and published in 1906. The Fondazione Rossini (Andrea Malnati, January 2026) judges that Rossini met only Beethoven’s brother in 1822 and never met Beethoven. The edge records the legend together with the Foundation’s verdict.

edges.claim: By the spring of 1828 [[rossini]] had already chosen William Tell as his next opera, but he wrote Le Comte Ory first so that he could reuse music from Il viaggio a Reims. Étienne de Jouy and Hippolyte Bis wrote the four-act French libretto from [[schiller]]’s play Wilhelm Tell (1804), and Guillaume Tell opened at the Académie Royale de Musique in Paris on 3 August 1829. The audience gave it a succès d’estime. Critics and musicians praised it, and Bellini called it his “musical bible”. It was Rossini’s last opera for the stage.

edges.title: Verdi’s proposed thirteen-composer Requiem for Rossini

works.from: Rossini’s death at Passy, 13 November 1868
works.to: Messa per Rossini, with Verdi’s Libera me (1869)

edges.claim: Four days after Rossini died, on 17 November 1868, [[verdi]] wrote to his publisher Ricordi proposing that “the most distinguished Italian composers” each set a section of a Requiem Mass for the anniversary of Rossini’s death, to be sealed in the archives of Bologna’s Liceo musicale once it had been performed. Verdi took the closing Libera me for himself. All thirteen composers delivered their movements, but the performance planned for San Petronio, Bologna, on 13 November 1869 never happened, and the Messa per Rossini was not heard until Helmuth Rilling conducted it at Stuttgart in September 1988. Verdi kept his Libera me and revised it for his own Messa da Requiem, first performed at Milan on 22 May 1874.

edges.title: Rossini’s influence on Bizet’s Prix de Rome years

works.from: Rossini’s operas, as Bizet knew them in Paris and at the Villa Medici
works.to: Bizet, Clovis et Clotilde (1857) and the Rome envois, 1858–60

edges.claim: The Palazzetto Bru Zane describes [[bizet]]’s Prix de Rome cantata Clovis et Clotilde, performed at the Institut on 3 October 1857, as nourished by the influences of Rossini, Meyerbeer and Gounod. At the Villa Medici, Hugh Macdonald writes, Bizet “had a lively taste for Italian music, especially Rossini”; he preferred Rossini, Mozart and Mendelssohn to Verdi, whose Un ballo in maschera he disliked. For his first Roman envoi he chose an Italian opera in place of the usual mass. On 25 June 1858 he wrote to his mother that he had found an Italian farce in the style of Don Pasquale and was “decidedly built for comic music”. The result was Don Procopio, an opera buffa wholly in the Italian manner.

edges.claim: Hugh Macdonald calls Gounod “certainly the leading influence” on the young [[bizet]]. The works that impressed him most were Sapho (1851), the choruses for Ulysse (1852) and Gounod’s First Symphony (1855). That year Bizet arranged the symphony for piano duet, and shortly after his seventeenth birthday he wrote his own Symphony in C, which Macdonald calls “clearly” modelled on Gounod’s. The autograph is dated 29 October–November 1855. The score lay forgotten until Felix Weingartner conducted it at Basel on 26 February 1935. In October 1872 Bizet wrote to Gounod: “You were the beginning of my life as an artist. I spring from you.”

The press condemned the libretto as absurd and the score as noisy and offensive, and Bizet counted the opera a failure. The best notice came from [[berlioz]], whose review in the Journal des débats on 8 October was his last feuilleton; it recognised the twenty-four-year-old as a serious talent with a great future. A few weeks later the same theatre staged Berlioz’s Les Troyens à Carthage, and Bizet offered to fight a duel in its defence.

edges.title: Tchaikovsky on Carmen and its future fame

works.from: Bizet, Carmen (1875): vocal score; Opéra-Comique, 20 January 1876

edges.claim: Tchaikovsky was studying the vocal score of Carmen, sent to him by Vladimir Shilovsky, by mid-1875, and heard the opera for the first time at the Opéra-Comique in Paris on 20 January 1876, with Célestine Galli-Marié in the title role. By the start of 1878 he had learnt nearly the whole of it by heart. In July 1880, staying at Nadezhda von Meck’s cottage at Simaki, he told her that to rest from his own music he had played Carmen through from beginning to end. He considered it a masterpiece “in the full sense” of the word, one of the few works fated to reflect most strongly the musical aspirations of a whole age. He was convinced that within ten years it would be the most popular opera in the world.

edges.title: Nietzsche hears Bizet’s Carmen in Genoa

works.from: Bizet, Carmen, Politeama Theatre, Genoa, 27 November 1881
works.to: Nietzsche, The Case of Wagner (1888)

edges.claim: On 27 November 1881 [[nietzsche]] heard Carmen for the first time, at the Politeama Theatre in Genoa. He wrote to his sister that he had been thunderstruck by an opera “so strong, so impassioned, so graceful, so Southern”, and he heard it again five days later. In The Case of Wagner (1888) he wrote that he had just heard Bizet’s masterpiece “for the twentieth time”, that Bizet’s orchestration was the only one he could still endure, and that this music was light and definite and free of grimaces, the opposite of Wagner’s “endless melody”.
